abstract: How neuronal ensembles determine the most relevant object to attend to remains unresolved but likely involves coordinating information across multiple brain areas. We found support for this hypothesis in latent firing co-variations across the prefrontal cortex (PFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and head of the caudate (CD) during and after attention-set learning. Before gaze shifted to an object, neuronal communication subspaces emerged across area pairs. While exploring options during learning, ACC and PFC led communication over the CD prior to gaze shifts, which switched to the CD and PFC leading the ACC when exploiting learned attention sets. Neurons participating in exploration- and exploitation-specific subspaces were partly segregated and carried information about the value and location of the to-be-selected objects, suggesting they guide attention and gaze.
